**PREDICTION:** If this is correct, you should see that whenever you ask for upfront payment, customers don't negotiate — they simply leave for another wholesaler, because you give them no other reason to stay.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be to build one advantage besides credit — for example, use your better-margin imported goods to stock items other Kikuubo wholesalers don't carry, so upcountry buyers come to you for products, not just for lending. The previous advisor treats credit as forced by competition, but that misses that you lose money on *specific* bad payers, not on credit itself.

**CAUSE:** Your problem is not that you give credit — it is that you give it to everyone the same way, without knowing who actually pays. You said "many of them delay" — meaning some do pay reliably and some do not, but you treat all buyers alike, so the bad ones drag you into "borrowing at high interest." You are only now starting a book of who owes you, which means until recently you had no way to tell a good buyer from a risky one.

**PREDICTION:** If this is correct, when you look at your new debt book you will see the same handful of names delaying again and again, while other buyers clear on time every trip.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be to sort your customers by their real payment history — give full credit only to those who have always paid, and demand your half-upfront rule strictly from the repeat late-payers.

**CAUSE:** Your trouble is a money-math problem, not a customer problem. Every trip your customers delay, the interest quietly swallows the little profit each basin or bucket was supposed to earn.

**PREDICTION:** If this is correct, you will notice that even customers who eventually pay in full leave you with almost no profit, because the loan interest you paid while waiting cancels out your margin on their goods.

**NEXT STEP:** Your priority should be to work out how much interest you pay per month of delay, then push your better-margin imported goods on credit and demand cash for low-margin local items — since only fatter margins can survive the waiting.
